learn.hook: You didn't invent the idea of school uniforms, marriage ceremonies or elections. They were waiting for you when you were born. Those lasting patterns are social institutions.
points: A social institution is a lasting pattern of norms, beliefs, values and roles organised around a social need, working by rules established by law or custom (family, economy, polity, religion, education).
Institutions constrain individuals (they set rules and limits) and also enable them (they open opportunities, like education opening careers).
Formal institutions are codified, e.g. law, the state and the education system; informal institutions rest on custom, e.g. family and religion in daily life.
Functionalist view: institutions meet society's needs and keep it stable. Conflict view: institutions tend to favour dominant groups and reproduce inequality.
Micro institutions (family) and macro institutions (state, economy) are interlinked: a change in one affects the others.

example.q: Show how the school both constrains and enables you.
steps: Constrains: fixed timings, uniforms, syllabus and exams limit what you can do.
Enables: literacy, certificates and skills open doors to jobs and higher studies.
So one institution both limits and empowers.
example.answer: School constrains through rules and timetables, but enables through knowledge and qualifications.

learn.reallife: Aadhaar, bank accounts and voter IDs show how state and economic institutions shape daily life: they set rules, but they also let you access schemes, loans and voting.

learn.hook: In one flat: Mummy, Papa and two kids. In the next: Dadi, Dada, two uncles, two aunts and five cousins. Both are families, and sociology wants to know why both survive in modern India.
points: Family: a group of people directly linked by kin connections, in which adult members take responsibility for caring for children.
Nuclear family: one set of parents and their children. Extended (joint) family: more than one couple and often more than two generations living together.
Functionalist view: the nuclear family was seen as best suited to industrial society because it is mobile and small.
Critique: in India the joint family has persisted and adapted, family forms change in many directions, and the 'nuclear = modern' idea is too simple.
Exam skill: compare features of nuclear and joint families (size, generations, authority, property, mobility).

example.q: Compare a nuclear and a joint family on size, generations and mobility.
steps: Size: nuclear is small; joint is larger.
Generations: nuclear usually two; joint often three or more, and more than one married couple.
Mobility: nuclear can move easily for jobs; joint is more rooted.
Both can exist side by side and change over a family's life cycle.
example.answer: Nuclear: small, two generations, mobile. Joint: larger, more than one couple and often three generations, less mobile.

topics.title: Family and other spheres; gender in the family

learn.hook: When a state suddenly withdraws family welfare, young couples may stop getting married. Family is never only private.
points: The family is linked to the economy, polity and culture; changes in one sphere affect the others.
Example: after the unification of Germany in 1990, the former East Germany saw marriage rates fall sharply, as state support for families was withdrawn and economic insecurity grew.
Gender inequality exists inside families: son preference leads to unequal care and can lead to sex-selective abortion, which is illegal in India.
India's child sex ratio (girls per 1,000 boys, age 0–6) fell from 945 in 1991 to 927 in 2001, a sign of son preference; campaigns like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao respond to this.
Exam skill: explain the relationship between the family and other spheres of social life.

example.q: India's child sex ratio fell from 945 (1991) to 927 (2001). By how much did it fall, and what does it indicate?
steps: Fall = 945 − 927 = 18 girls per 1,000 boys.
A falling child sex ratio indicates son preference and discrimination against girls.
It links family values with technology (sex-determination) and law (the PCPNDT Act bans sex selection).
example.answer: It fell by 18 points, indicating son preference within families.

learn.reallife: Haryana's campaigns under Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, launched from Panipat in 2015, targeted districts with low child sex ratios, showing state action on a family-level inequality.

learn.hook: Among the Khasi of Meghalaya, the youngest daughter traditionally inherits the ancestral house. In many other communities, it goes to sons. Family rules differ more than you think.
points: By residence: patrilocal (the couple lives with the husband's family) and matrilocal (the couple lives with the wife's family).
By descent and inheritance: patrilineal (property and name pass from father to son) and matrilineal (from mother to daughter).

By authority: patriarchal (men hold authority and dominance) and matriarchal (women hold dominance). Matriarchy remains largely a theoretical idea; even in matrilineal societies, authority is often held by men such as the mother's brother.
Examples: the Khasi of Meghalaya and the Nairs of Kerala (historically) are matrilineal communities.
Activity skill: map your own family's kinship terms and residence pattern, and compare family forms across regions.

example.q: In a community, a married couple lives with the wife's mother, property passes to daughters, but the wife's brother makes major decisions. Classify it.
steps: Living with wife's family: matrilocal.

So matriliny need not mean matriarchy.
example.answer: Matrilocal and matrilineal, but not matriarchal: authority still lies with a man.

learn.reallife: In Meghalaya, Khasi children traditionally take the mother's clan name, while in most of north India children take the father's surname, a visible sign of descent rules.

learn.hook: One spouse for life, one spouse at a time, or more than one at once: societies across the world have organised marriage in all these ways.
points: Marriage is a socially sanctioned, often legally recognised, union between partners, creating rights and duties.
Monogamy: one spouse at a time. Serial monogamy: remarrying after the death of a spouse or after divorce, but still one spouse at a time.
Polygamy: more than one spouse at a time. Its two types are polygyny (one husband, two or more wives) and polyandry (one wife, two or more husbands).
Polyandry has been linked with harsh economic conditions and scarce land, e.g. fraternal polyandry (brothers sharing a wife) in some Himalayan regions, which keeps land undivided.
In India, the law today generally requires monogamy for most communities (e.g. under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955).

example.q: Classify: (a) Ram marries Sita after his first wife died; (b) a man with three wives at once; (c) a woman married to two brothers; (d) a couple married for 40 years.
steps: (a) one spouse at a time after a death: serial monogamy.
(b) one husband, many wives: polygyny.
(c) one wife, many husbands (brothers): fraternal polyandry.
(d) one spouse: monogamy.
example.answer: (a) serial monogamy, (b) polygyny, (c) fraternal polyandry, (d) monogamy.

topics.title: Transformation of work: Fordism to flexible production

learn.hook: In Henry Ford's factory, a worker might tighten the same bolt all day. Today, a T-shirt sold in London may be stitched in Tiruppur, designed in Paris and shipped from Singapore.
points: Scientific management (F.W. Taylor): break each job into simple timed tasks and supervise closely to raise efficiency.
Fordism (Henry Ford): mass production of standard goods on moving assembly lines, with large factories and a mass market.
Flexible production (post-Fordism): small batches tailored to changing demand, outsourcing parts of production to other firms and countries, enabled by globalisation.
Example: garment workers in countries like India and Bangladesh produce clothes for global retailers under subcontracting chains.
Work has become more insecure: low wages, contract and casual labour, and a decline of permanent jobs with benefits.

example.q: Trace how producing a shirt changed from a Fordist factory to flexible production.
steps: Fordist: one huge factory, assembly line, standard design, long production runs.
Flexible: brand designs centrally, outsources cutting and stitching to subcontractors abroad.
Orders change quickly with fashion; small batches.
Workers in subcontracting units often have temporary contracts and low wages.
example.answer: From one giant assembly-line factory to globally outsourced, small-batch production with more insecure work.

learn.hook: A robber with a knife and a traffic constable can both make you stop. Only one has authority. What's the difference?
points: Political institutions are concerned with the acquisition and distribution of power in society.
Power (in Max Weber's sense): the ability of individuals or groups to carry out their will even against the resistance of others. Seen as a fixed quantity: if one has more, another has less.
Authority is legitimate power: power accepted as just and proper by those it is exercised over.
Stateless societies have no formal state, yet maintain order through kinship, age-sets (groups of people of similar age who move through life stages together), rituals and cross-cutting ties.

topics.title: The state, sovereignty, citizenship and nationalism

learn.hook: Your passport says 'Republic of India'. Behind that small book lie big ideas: a state, sovereignty, citizenship and a nation.
points: The state: a political apparatus (government, civil service, police, army) ruling over a defined territory, with authority backed by a legal system and the capacity to use force.
Functionalist view: the state serves the interests of all of society. Conflict view: the state tends to represent the interests of dominant classes.
Sovereignty: undisputed political rule of a state over a given territory.

Citizenship: membership of a political community, with rights and duties. Rights are often classed (following T.H. Marshall) as civil (free speech, equality before law, property), political (vote, contest elections) and social (welfare, health, education, minimum income).
Nationalism: a sense of belonging to a political community. Struggles by excluded groups (workers, women, Dalits, minorities) have expanded citizenship rights and democracy.

learn.hook: A theologian asks 'Is this belief true?'. A sociologist asks 'What does this belief do for the people who hold it, and how does it shape society?'
points: The sociological study of religion is empirical (based on observation), comparative (across religions and societies) and non-judgemental; it does not ask which religion is true, unlike theology.
Common features of religion: a set of shared beliefs and rituals, sacred symbols, and a community of believers.
Emile Durkheim distinguished the sacred (set apart, treated with awe and reverence) from the profane (the ordinary, everyday world).

example.answer: (a) and (c) are sacred; (b) and (d) are profane: meaning, not the object, decides.

learn.hook: At home you are 'Chintu', the family's darling. At school you are Roll No. 23, judged by the same rules as everyone else. That shift is a big lesson in itself.
points: Education is a lifelong process of learning; schooling is its formal, institutionalised form (with set curricula, teachers and certificates).
Emile Durkheim saw education as transmitting society's shared norms and values, creating the common bonds a society needs to survive.
In simple societies, children learn through daily community life; complex societies need formal schooling because knowledge and skills are specialised.
Schools teach universalistic values (the same rules and standards for everyone) in contrast to the particularistic values of the family (treating a person as special because of a relationship).

At school: every answer sheet is marked on the same scheme regardless of who you are (universalistic).
School thus prepares children for a society governed by impersonal, common rules.
example.answer: Families judge by relationship (particularistic); schools apply the same standards to all (universalistic).
